title: Adders — from one bit to a four-bit sum
subtitle: Binary addition, the half and full adder, the ripple-carry chain, and the same circuit made to subtract. Every figure is a live logic circuit; every truth table is generated by simulating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
A processor adds more often than it does anything else. Every loop counter, every array index, every multiply built from shifts and adds, every address the memory bus ever sees — all of it is addition. And the machine doing it has no concept of a number: it has wires that are either near the supply rail or near ground, and gates that combine them.

These notes build the adder up from that floor. First the four one-bit sums, then the half adder that produces them, then the full adder that can be chained, then a four-bit adder that carries a result from one stage to the next — and finally the same circuit made to subtract, and to drive a digit onto a display.

How to read these notesEvery circuit here is live. Each one carries its own Simulate button: press it and the logic solver runs that circuit, the output indicators show 0 or 1, and the sliders beneath change the inputs while it runs. A truth table under a figure is not typed out — it is produced by simulating that exact circuit for every input combination.
What this simulator does not model. Its logic pass settles instantly: it finds the stable value of every wire and stops. Real gates take time, and §9 is entirely about that time — but the figures there cannot show it, and the notes say so where it matters rather than pretending otherwise.

sections.eyebrow: The whole problem, in four lines
sections.title: Adding two bits
sections.body:
Binary addition has exactly four cases, and three of them are trivial. 0 + 0 is 0. 0 + 1 and 1 + 0 are both 1. The fourth case is where the hardware comes from: 1 + 1 is two, and two is not a digit in binary. It is written 10 — a 0 in this column and a 1 carried into the next.

So a one-bit adder cannot have one output. It needs two: the sum bit that stays in this column, and the carry bit that moves left. Everything else in this lesson follows from that single fact.

choices.text: 10 — a sum bit of 0 and a carry of 1.
2 — the same as in decimal, just written in a binary circuit.
1 — there is no digit above 1, so the result saturates.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Two needs two bits. The right-hand column keeps 0 and the 1 moves one place left, exactly as 5 + 5 = 10 does in decimal: the column overflows and a carry goes next door. The circuit below computes both halves of that answer at once.

responses.title: There is no digit 2 to write.
responses.body: Binary has two symbols, 0 and 1, and the value two is spelled 10. A wire can carry either level and nothing between, so a '2' is not something the hardware could represent even if the arithmetic wanted it.

responses.title: Nothing saturates — the value goes somewhere.
responses.body: Saturation is a design choice some arithmetic units make deliberately, but plain addition does not lose the overflow: it carries it into the next column. Discarding it is what produces the wrap-around of §10, and even there the bit exists and is visible on the carry output.

verify.caption: Verify — a one-bit adder with both inputs at 1
verify.note: Press Simulate. The sum output S reads 0 and the carry output C reads 1 — the two bits of the answer 10.

questions.prompt: Which single gate gives the SUM bit of a one-bit addition?

choices.text: XOR — it is 1 when exactly one input is 1.
OR — addition means 'either one or the other contributes'.
AND — both inputs have to be present for a result.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Compare the two columns: the sum bit is 0, 1, 1, 0 as the inputs run 00, 01, 10, 11 — and that is the XOR truth table exactly. The last row is the only one where they differ from OR, and it is the row that matters.

responses.title: OR agrees on three rows out of four, and fails the one that counts.
responses.body: For 1 + 1 an OR gate gives 1, but the sum bit of 1 + 1 is 0 — the 1 belongs in the carry. Run the circuit below: an OR gate with both inputs at 1 reads 1, which is the wrong sum bit. XOR is OR with that one row corrected.

responses.title: AND is the CARRY, not the sum.
responses.body: AND is 1 only when both inputs are 1, which is precisely when a carry is generated — so the intuition is right, aimed at the wrong output. The half adder below uses both: XOR for the sum and AND for the carry.

verify.caption: Verify — an OR gate cannot be the sum bit
verify.note: Press Simulate: OUT reads 1 for 1 + 1, but the sum bit of 1 + 1 is 0. This gate is right on three rows and wrong on the fourth.

figures.caption: Figure 2.1 — every one-bit addition there is
figures.script: var tbl = create("table", { headers: "A;B;Carry;Sum;Value", data: [[0, 0, 0, 0, "0"], [0, 1, 0, 1, "1"], [1, 0, 0, 1, "1"], [1, 1, 1, 0, "2 (written 10)"]], summary: "None" });
figures.note: Read the Sum column downward: 0, 1, 1, 0. Now read the Carry column: 0, 0, 0, 1. Each is a familiar gate.

sections.after: Four rows is the entire specification of a one-bit adder. The rest of this lesson is that specification implemented, chained, and then bent into doing subtraction.

sections.title: The half adder
sections.body:
Wire an XOR gate and an AND gate across the same two inputs and you have a half adder: the XOR produces the sum bit, the AND produces the carry. Two gates, two inputs, two outputs, and it implements Figure 2.1 completely.

The truth table under the circuit is not typed into these notes. It is generated by driving that exact circuit through all four input combinations and reading what comes out, so if the wiring were wrong the table would be wrong in the same way — which is the only kind of table worth printing beside a circuit.

figures.caption: Figure 3.1 — a half adder, and the table its own circuit produces
figures.note: Press Simulate, then drag the A and B sliders. With both at 1 the sum output S reads 0 and the carry C reads 1. The table below is simulated from this circuit, one run per row.

sections.after:
Now try to use it. Adding two four-bit numbers means four columns, and every column but the rightmost has three bits arriving: the two input bits and the carry out of the column to its right. A half adder has two inputs. There is nowhere to put the carry.

That is what the name means. It is half of what a column of a real addition needs — and it is exactly right for the one column that has no carry coming in, the least significant.

questions.prompt: Why is it called a HALF adder?

choices.text: It has no carry input, so it can only serve the rightmost column of an addition.
It produces half of the answer — the sum bit — and another circuit produces the carry.
It uses half the gates of a full adder, which is the only difference.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It takes two bits, and a column in the middle of an addition has three: A, B and the carry arriving from the right. The half adder is complete for the least significant column and unusable for every other one.

responses.title: It produces both output bits already.
responses.body: Sum and carry both come out of the half adder — that is the whole circuit in Figure 3.1. What it cannot do is ACCEPT a carry, which is a missing input rather than a missing output.

responses.title: The gate count is a consequence, not the reason.
responses.body: A full adder is indeed bigger, but the name is about the job: 'half' of a column's work, because a column in general has three incoming bits. Sizing follows from that, not the other way around.

verify.caption: Verify — the missing input, supplied
verify.note: This is a full adder: the same A and B, plus a carry in. With all three at 1 the sum S reads 1 and the carry out reads 1 — the answer 11, which is three. No half adder can express this.

sections.eyebrow: From the table to the gates
sections.title: Reading the circuit off the truth table
sections.body: Figure 3.1 was presented as a finished circuit, which is the wrong way round: the table comes first and the gates are derived from it. Doing that derivation properly is the skill the rest of combinational design rests on.

derivation.why: A truth table with two outputs is two independent problems. The sum column and the carry column each get their own expression, and each is built from the rows where that output is 1 — the rows where it is 0 need no term, because a sum of products is 0 unless one of its products fires.

Carry is 1 in exactly one row, A = 1 and B = 1. One row means one product term, and that term is the AND of the inputs in the state that row gives them. This is why the carry needs a single AND gate and nothing else.

derivation.toc: The sum column, the long way
derivation.why: Sum is 1 in two rows: A = 0 with B = 1, and A = 1 with B = 0. Written directly as a sum of products, each row contributes the AND of its inputs with the 0s inverted.

That expression — true when the inputs differ, false when they agree — is exclusive-OR, and a single gate implements it. Recognising a standard function in a sum of products is what turns four gates and two inverters into one, and it is worth doing before reaching for a Karnaugh map.
Both outputs, from the same two inputs. Nothing is shared between them — the XOR and the AND look at the same wires and work independently, which is why both results appear at the same time.
derivation.math: S = A \oplus B, \qquad C = A \cdot B

problems.prompt: A designer has only NAND gates. Show how the CARRY output of a half adder is built from them, and say how many are needed.
problems.answer:
A NAND is an AND followed by an inverter, so undoing the inversion restores the AND. Feed A and B into the first NAND, then feed its output into a second NAND with both of its inputs tied together — a two-input NAND with the same signal on both inputs is an inverter.

So two NAND gates: one to compute the inverted AND, one to invert it back. This is not a curiosity. NAND is functionally complete — every Boolean function can be built from NAND alone — and a fabrication process that only has to make one kind of gate well is a cheaper process.

problems.prompt: Using the sum-of-products form S = A̅B + AB̅ literally, how many gates does the sum bit cost? Compare that with the XOR form.
problems.answer:
Written literally it needs two inverters (for A̅ and B̅), two AND gates (one per product term) and one OR gate to combine them: five gates.

As a single XOR it costs one — which at the transistor level is not quite the bargain it looks, since an XOR is internally several transistors, but at the schematic level it is the difference between a readable adder and an unreadable one. Recognising the pattern is worth more than minimising the literal expression.

sections.title: The full adder
sections.body:
A column in the middle of an addition receives three bits: A, B and the carry out of the column to its right. Their total runs from 0 to 3, which still fits in two output bits — a sum and a carry — so the shape of the circuit does not change. Only the input count does.

A circuit that adds three bits and produces a two-bit result is a full adder, and it is the unit every wider adder is built from. Three inputs means eight rows, and the table below is again generated by running the circuit rather than by asserting it.

questions.prompt: How many rows does a full adder's truth table have?

choices.text: 8 — two possibilities for each of three inputs.
6 — three inputs, each of which can be 0 or 1.
4 — the same four cases as the half adder, since the carry just passes through.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each input doubles the table: 2³ = 8. This is also why truth tables stop being the right tool quickly — a four-bit adder has eight inputs and 256 rows, which is why §7 reasons about structure instead.

responses.title: This adds where it should multiply.
responses.body: Three inputs with two states each give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations, not 3 × 2 = 6. The count doubles per input, which is exactly why an exhaustive table becomes impractical so fast.

responses.title: The carry in does not pass through — it is added.
responses.body: With A = 1, B = 1 and a carry in of 1 the total is three, which is not what A + B alone gives. Every one of the eight combinations is a distinct input to the arithmetic, so none of them can be folded away.

questions.prompt: A full adder has A = 1, B = 0 and a carry in of 1. What are its outputs?

choices.text: Sum 0, carry out 1 — the total is two.
Sum 1, carry out 1 — both inputs that are 1 show up on both outputs.
Sum 0, carry out 0 — the two 1s cancel in the XOR.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: sum 0, carry 1. The rule is simply the total of the three input bits written in two bits — count the 1s, write the count.

responses.title: That answer is three, not two.
responses.body: Sum 1 with carry 1 spells 11, and three ones would be needed to reach it. Two of the inputs are 1 here and one is 0, so the total is two.

responses.title: The XOR is right; the carry is missing.
responses.body: A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin does give 0 here, so the sum bit is correct — but two of the three inputs are 1, so a carry must leave the column. A sum of 0 with no carry would be claiming the total is zero.

verify.caption: Verify — 1 + 0 + 1 in one column
verify.note: Press Simulate: the sum output reads 0 and the carry out reads 1.

derivation.why: The sum bit is 1 whenever an ODD number of inputs is 1 — rows 001, 010, 100 and 111. Odd-parity of several bits is chained XOR, so the two-input sum of the half adder simply extends.
A carry leaves the column when at least two of the three inputs are 1. Written out one pair at a time, that is any of the three pairs being both-1.

The two terms containing Cin share it, and A + B in that context is the same as A ⊕ B (the case where both are 1 is already covered by the AB term, so either spelling gives the same output). This form matters because it reuses the A ⊕ B the sum bit already computes — the same wire feeds both, which is what makes the two-half-adder construction of §6 possible.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1 — a full adder and its eight rows
figures.note: Press Simulate and work the three sliders. With all three inputs at 1 the sum reads 1 and the carry out reads 1 — three, written 11. Check any row of the table against the rule 'count the 1s, write the count in two bits'.

sections.title: A full adder from two half adders
sections.body:
The factored carry expression, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), says something structural: everything a full adder needs is already produced by two half adders. The first adds A and B. The second adds that partial sum to the carry in. Each one hands over its own carry, and the two carries are ORed together.

The OR is safe because the two carries can never both be 1. If the first half adder carried, its sum bit was 0, so the second half adder had 0 + Cin and cannot carry. Only one of the two can fire in any row, which is why an OR — rather than a second adder — finishes the job.

questions.prompt: Why can the two half adders' carry outputs simply be ORed together?

choices.text: They can never both be 1, so OR just passes whichever one fired.
Because OR is the same as addition for single bits.
Because only the first half adder can ever produce a carry.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: If the first carried, A and B were both 1 and its sum bit is 0 — so the second half adder sees 0 + Cin and cannot carry. The two are mutually exclusive, and for mutually exclusive signals OR and addition agree.

responses.title: OR is addition everywhere except the row that matters.
responses.body: 1 OR 1 is 1, but 1 + 1 is two — which is the whole reason a carry exists. The construction works here not because OR adds, but because the case where they differ cannot occur.

responses.title: The second one can carry, and often does.
responses.body: Take A = 1, B = 0, Cin = 1: the first half adder gives sum 1, carry 0; the second adds 1 + 1 and carries. The carry in the answer comes from the SECOND half adder in that row.

verify.caption: Verify — the second half adder carrying
verify.note: A = 1, B = 0, carry in 1: sum 0, carry out 1. The first stage produced no carry at all here; the carry you can see came from the second.

figures.caption: Figure 6.1 — one full adder, built from two half adders and an OR gate
figures.note: Press Simulate and drive the three sliders. It behaves identically to Figure 5.1 — same eight rows — because it computes the same two expressions.

figures.caption: Figure 6.2 — the structure, without the wires
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
((A)) as a #grey
((B)) as b #grey
((Cin)) as ci #grey
[Half adder 1] as h1 #blue
[Half adder 2] as h2 #blue
[OR] as og #amber
((Sum)) as s #mint
((Carry out)) as co #mint
a -> h1
b -> h1
h1 -> h2 : partial sum
ci -> h2
h2 -> s
h1 -> og : carry 1
h2 -> og : carry 2
og -> co");
figures.note: The partial sum crosses from the first stage to the second; the two carries meet at the OR. Compare it with the wiring above — this is the same circuit with the gate detail removed.

sections.after: Which one does hardware actually use? Neither shape is sacred. A standard-cell library implements the full adder as one optimised cell, chosen for its carry delay rather than its tidiness on paper, because the carry path is what sets the speed of everything built from it — which is §9.

sections.title: The ripple-carry adder
sections.body:
Chaining is now mechanical. One full adder per bit; each one's carry output becomes the next one's carry input; the rightmost carry input is 0, because nothing is carried into the least significant column. The carry out of the leftmost stage is the ninth bit of an eight-bit answer — or, for our four-bit adder, the fifth bit of a five-bit answer.

The circuit below adds A = 1011 (eleven) and B = 0110 (six). Seventeen does not fit in four bits, so the sum outputs read 0001 and the carry out reads 1: together, 10001, which is seventeen.

Set your own numbersPress Simulate, then use the eight sliders. A3 is the most significant bit of A and A0 the least; the same for B. Watch which output bits change when you flip A0 — a carry from the bottom can alter every bit above it.

questions.prompt: In a ripple-carry adder, which sum bit is correct first after the inputs change?

choices.text: S0, the least significant — it waits for no carry.
S3, the most significant — the carry chain is evaluated from the left.
All of them at once, because the gates all switch together.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Column 0's carry in is fixed at 0, so S0 depends only on A0 and B0 and settles after one gate delay. Every bit above it must wait for the carry to arrive from its right, which is precisely the ripple the name describes.

responses.title: The carry moves right-to-left, like a hand-worked sum.
responses.body: The most significant column is the LAST to know — it cannot decide its output until the carry has passed through every stage below it. That is what makes it the slowest bit and the one that sets the adder's speed.

responses.title: They switch together only in a model with no delay.
responses.body: This simulator's logic pass does settle instantly, so the figures cannot show the difference — but in silicon each gate takes time, and the carry has to cross them one after another. §9 puts numbers on it.

questions.prompt: The four-bit adder is given 1111 (fifteen) and 0001 (one). What do the four sum outputs read?

choices.text: 0000, with the carry out at 1.
1111, because the adder saturates at its largest value.
10000 — the adder widens itself to hold the answer.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Sixteen needs five bits. The four sum outputs hold the bottom four, all zero, and the sixteen appears on the carry out. Nothing is lost as long as you read the carry — it is only lost if you ignore it, which is the whole subject of §10.

responses.title: Saturation is a thing some circuits do, and this is not one of them.
responses.body: Saturating arithmetic (clamping at the maximum instead of wrapping) exists in DSP and graphics hardware, and it costs extra logic to detect and force the clamp. A plain ripple-carry adder wraps: it computes modulo 16 and hands you the overflow on a separate pin.

responses.title: The hardware is a fixed width; it cannot grow a bit.
responses.body: Four full adders have four sum outputs, and no input pattern changes that. The fifth bit of the answer exists, but it is the carry output — a separate wire that the next stage, or the status register, has to be wired to.

verify.caption: Verify — fifteen plus one, in four bits
verify.note: Press Simulate: S3 S2 S1 S0 all read 0 and the carry out reads 1. The answer is 10000 — sixteen — spread across five pins.

figures.caption: Figure 7.1 — a four-bit ripple-carry adder, 1011 + 0110
figures.note: Press Simulate. S3 S2 S1 S0 read 0001 and the carry out reads 1 — seventeen. Then set B to 0001 and step A up from 0000 with the sliders to watch the carry travel.

figures.caption: Figure 7.2 — how the stages are chained
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
[Stage 0 A0 B0] as f0 #blue
[Stage 1 A1 B1] as f1 #blue
[Stage 2 A2 B2] as f2 #blue
[Stage 3 A3 B3] as f3 #blue
((Carry out)) as co #mint
f0 -> f1 : C1
f1 -> f2 : C2
f2 -> f3 : C3
f3 -> co : C4");
figures.note: Each arrow is one wire: the carry. The sum bits leave downward from each stage and are not drawn — nothing downstream depends on them, which is exactly why the carry chain alone sets the speed.

sections.title: Worked example — 1011 + 0110
sections.body:
Add the two four-bit numbers of Figure 7.1 by hand, column by column, then check every bit against the circuit.

Each step is revealed one at a time. Work the column yourself before opening the next.

worked.why: Column 0 (the least significant). A0 = 1, B0 = 0, and the carry in is 0 because nothing is carried into the rightmost column. One 1 among the three inputs: sum 1, no carry.
Column 1. A1 = 1, B1 = 1, carry in 0. Two 1s: the total is two, which is 10 — the sum bit is 0 and a carry goes to column 2.
Column 2. A2 = 0, B2 = 1, and now the carry in is 1. Two 1s again: sum 0, carry 1. This is the column where the ripple matters — its answer could not be computed until column 1 finished.
Column 3 (the most significant). A3 = 1, B3 = 0, carry in 1. Two 1s: sum 0, and the carry leaves the adder entirely.
Read the answer. The sum outputs spell 0001 and the carry out is 1, so the full five-bit result is 10001. In decimal that is 16 + 1 = 17, and 11 + 6 = 17 — the arithmetic checks.

Check it against the circuit. Figure 7.1 reads S3 S2 S1 S0 = 0001 with the carry out at 1 — the same five bits, computed by four full adders rather than by hand. If your columns and the circuit ever disagree, the carry chain is where to look first: an error in column 1 silently poisons every column above it.

problems.prompt: Add 1010 and 0011 in four bits. Give the sum bits and the carry out, and check the answer in decimal.
problems.answer:
Column 0: 0 + 1 + 0 = 1, so S0 = 1, no carry. Column 1: 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, so S1 = 0 and a carry goes up. Column 2: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, so S2 = 1, no carry. Column 3: 1 + 0 + 0 = 1, so S3 = 1.

The result is 1101 with a carry out of 0. In decimal, 10 + 3 = 13, and 1101 is 13 — it fits in four bits, which is exactly what the zero carry out is telling you.

verify.caption: Verify — 1010 + 0011
verify.note: S3 S2 S1 S0 read 1101 and the carry out reads 0.

problems.prompt: You need a circuit that adds one to a four-bit number — an incrementer for a program counter. Using nothing but the adder you already have, how do you wire it?
problems.answer:
Tie all four B inputs to 0 and set the carry in to 1. The adder then computes A + 0 + 1 = A + 1, and the carry in — usually the dull pin that exists only for chaining — is doing the whole job.

The verify circuit is that wiring with A = 0110 (six): the outputs read 0111, seven. In real hardware you would not pay for four full adders to do this; an incrementer is built from half adders, since one of the two operands is known to be zero at every bit. But the trick of feeding a constant through the carry in is worth keeping — it is also how the subtractor in §11 gets its +1.

verify.caption: Verify — an adder wired as an incrementer
verify.note: A = 0110, every B input at 0, carry in 1. The sum outputs read 0111 — six plus one.

sections.title: Propagation delay and the carry path
sections.body:
Every gate takes time. Its output does not change at the instant its input does; it changes one propagation delay later, once the transistors inside have charged the next stage's input capacitance. Call that delay Δ and assume for now that every gate has the same one — a crude model, but the right one for comparing structures.

The sum outputs of a ripple-carry adder are not the problem. The carry is. It enters stage 0, leaves it, enters stage 1, and so on: the stages cannot work in parallel, because each one's answer depends on the one below it. The adder is not finished when its slowest gate is finished — it is finished when the carry has crossed every stage.

derivation.why: Every gate switches in Δ. The full adder is the two-half-adder circuit of §6, so its internal paths are: carry in to carry out passes an AND then an OR, which is 2Δ; an input A or B to carry out passes an XOR, an AND and an OR, which is 3Δ. These two numbers are the whole calculation. The equal-delay assumption is the approximation here — a real XOR is slower than a real NAND — and it is stated because everything below inherits it.
Stage 0's carry comes from its own A and B inputs, so it appears 3Δ after the inputs are applied. That carry is what the rest of the chain waits for.
From then on each stage only has to get an already-settled carry from its input to its output, which is the 2Δ path. Stage k's carry therefore appears 2Δ after stage k−1's.

Add them up for an n-bit adder: 3Δ to produce the first carry, then 2Δ per stage for the remaining n−1 stages. The result is LINEAR in the width, which is the defining property of ripple-carry — and the reason it is abandoned for wide, fast datapaths.

questions.prompt: A 16-bit ripple-carry adder is replaced by a 32-bit one, built the same way. Roughly what happens to its worst-case delay?

choices.text: It doubles — the delay grows in proportion to the width.
It quadruples — twice the bits means twice the carries, each taking twice as long.
It barely changes — the stages operate in parallel, so width is nearly free.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: (2n + 1)Δ is linear in n: 33Δ becomes 65Δ, a shade under double. This is the honest cost of the simplest possible structure, and it is why carry-lookahead — which computes each stage's carry from the inputs directly instead of waiting for its neighbour — exists at all.

responses.title: Each carry still takes the same 2Δ.
responses.body: The number of stages doubles, but a stage does not get slower because the adder got wider. Doubling one factor doubles the product; nothing here squares.

responses.title: The sum bits are parallel; the carry is not.
responses.body: That is the seductive part of the picture: all four (or thirty-two) full adders really do sit there working at once. But each one is working on a carry that has not arrived yet, and its output is meaningless until it does. A chain of dependencies cannot be parallel, however much hardware you put beside it.

questions.prompt: Figure 7.1 shows the correct answer the instant it is simulated. What does that tell you about the propagation delay of a real adder?

choices.text: Nothing — this simulator's logic pass settles instantly and models no delay at all.
That the delay is too small to matter in a four-bit adder.
That the carry really does arrive everywhere at once, and delay only appears in much wider adders.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The logic solver here finds the stable state of every wire and stops; there is no time axis in it. That is a deliberate limit, not a claim about hardware — and it is why this section reasons with Δ on paper instead of pointing at a figure. A simulator that shows you a result instantly has told you what the answer is, not when it arrives.

responses.title: Thirteen and a half nanoseconds is not nothing.
responses.body: At 1.5 ns per gate a four-bit ripple adder settles in 13.5 ns, which caps a circuit built around it at about 74 MHz. The figure shows no delay because the model has none, not because the delay is negligible.

responses.title: The carry is the one signal that provably does not arrive at once.
responses.body: Each stage's carry is computed from the stage below it, so stage 3 cannot know its carry until stages 0 to 2 have switched in turn. The figures are silent about this because their solver has no notion of time, not because the hardware is.

figures.caption: Figure 9.1 — the critical path is the carry, not the sum
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
((A0 B0)) as in0 #grey
[Stage 0] as f0 #blue
[Stage 1] as f1 #blue
[Stage 2] as f2 #blue
[Stage 3] as f3 #blue
((S3 valid)) as done #mint
[S0 valid after 2 delta] as s0 #mint
in0 -> f0 : inputs applied
f0 -> s0 : sum path
f0 -> f1 : 3 delta
f1 -> f2 : + 2 delta
f2 -> f3 : + 2 delta
f3 -> done : 9 delta");
figures.note: The lower branch finishes almost immediately; the upper one is a chain nothing can shorten. An adder's speed is the length of its longest dependency, never the average one.

problems.prompt: Each gate in a library switches in 1.5 ns. How long after its inputs settle is an 8-bit ripple-carry adder's result trustworthy?
problems.answer:
Use t = (2n + 1)Δ with n = 8: t = 17 × 1.5 = 25.5 ns.

"Trustworthy" is the operative word. Every output pin carries some value from the moment power is applied; what changes at 25.5 ns is that the values stop being garbage left over from the carries still in flight. A register clocked earlier than that latches a number that was never the sum of anything.

problems.prompt: A 32-bit ripple-carry adder is placed between two registers in a design with the same 1.5 ns gates. Ignoring every other delay, what is the highest clock frequency this datapath can run at?
problems.answer:
t = (2 × 32 + 1) × 1.5 = 65 × 1.5 = 97.5 ns, so fmax = 1 / 97.5 ns ≈ 10.3 MHz.

That number is the argument for every fast-adder structure ever designed. A processor clocked at 1 GHz has one nanosecond per cycle, and this adder alone wants ninety-seven of them — so its carries cannot be allowed to ripple. Carry-lookahead computes the carry into every stage directly from the inputs, in a fixed number of gate delays regardless of width, and pays for it in gates.

Note also what "ignoring every other delay" hides: register setup time, clock skew and wire delay all eat into the same budget, so the real ceiling is lower than 10.3 MHz, never higher.

sections.eyebrow: When four bits are not enough
sections.title: Carry out, and what it does not tell you
sections.body:
The carry out of the top stage answers one question: did the unsigned result need a fifth bit? For unsigned numbers that is the whole story — carry out 1 means the answer was too big for the width, and the value on the sum pins is the true answer modulo 16.

For signed numbers it is the wrong question. In two's complement the top bit is the sign, so a four-bit register holds −8 to +7, and the interesting failure is a result that leaves that range. Add 0111 (seven) and 0001 (one): the sum pins read 1000 and the carry out is 0. No carry left the adder, and the answer is still wrong — 1000 read as signed is −8.

The detector for signed overflow is different: overflow is the carry into the top stage disagreeing with the carry out of it, V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1. Equivalently, and more memorably: adding two numbers of the same sign and getting the opposite sign is always overflow, and adding opposite signs can never overflow.

questions.prompt: A four-bit adder computes 0111 + 0001. Reading the operands as signed numbers, what has happened?

choices.text: Signed overflow: 7 + 1 gives 1000, which reads as −8, and the carry out is 0.
Nothing unusual — the carry out is 0, so the result fits.
Unsigned overflow: the result needs a fifth bit, which appears on the carry out.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Two positive numbers produced a negative one — the definitive symptom. The carry out is 0 and is no help at all here, which is exactly why a separate overflow flag exists in every processor's status register alongside the carry flag.

responses.title: The carry out answers the UNSIGNED question.
responses.body: As unsigned numbers, 7 + 1 = 8 fits in four bits perfectly and the zero carry out is telling the truth. As signed numbers +8 does not exist in four bits, and the pins read −8. One result, two readings, two different verdicts — the hardware computes both flags and lets the program decide which one it meant.

responses.title: Nothing left the top of the adder.
responses.body: Run it: the carry out pin reads 0. The fifth bit was not needed, because 8 fits in four bits as an unsigned value. The failure here is entirely about interpretation, which no carry pin can see.

verify.caption: Verify — 0111 + 0001 in four bits
verify.note: Press Simulate: the sum outputs read 1000 and the carry out reads 0. As unsigned that is eight and correct; as signed it is −8 and wrong.

questions.prompt: Can adding a positive number and a negative number ever overflow a signed adder?

choices.text: No — the magnitude of the result is never larger than the larger operand.
Yes, whenever the negative number is larger in magnitude.
Yes, whenever a carry leaves the top stage.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The result lies between the two operands, and both of them already fit in the width, so the result must too. Overflow needs same-signed operands — which is why the ⊕ of the top two carries detects it: those two carries can only differ when the operands' signs agree and the answer's does not.

responses.title: A bigger negative just gives a negative result.
responses.body: −5 + 3 = −2, and −2 is comfortably representable. Nothing about the magnitudes can push the answer outside a range that already contains both of them.

responses.title: A carry out of the top stage is routine in signed arithmetic.
responses.body: Adding two negatives in two's complement almost always produces a carry out, and the result is usually perfectly correct. The carry pin means overflow for UNSIGNED operands only; for signed ones the flag to read is V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1.

problems.prompt: Four-bit signed addition: 0110 + 0101. Give the sum bits, the carry out, and say whether the result is usable.
problems.answer:
Six plus five is eleven, and 1011 is what the pins read, with a carry out of 0. As unsigned that is correct — eleven fits in four bits. As signed it is overflow: two positives have produced 1011, which reads as −5.

The check by carries: the carry into the top stage is 1 (columns 0-2 produce 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 0 = 1, then 1 + 1 = carry) while the carry out of it is 0, so V = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. The flag fires even though the carry pin stays quiet.

verify.caption: Verify — 0110 + 0101
verify.note: The sum outputs read 1011 and the carry out reads 0. Which of those two readings is 'right' depends entirely on what the programmer intended the bits to mean.

problems.prompt: How many distinct values can a four-bit adder's five output pins represent, and what is the largest sum two four-bit unsigned inputs can produce? Does the hardware ever lose a result?
problems.answer:
Five pins represent 32 values, 0 to 31. The largest sum of two four-bit unsigned numbers is 15 + 15 = 30, and with a carry in of 1 it reaches 31 — exactly the top of the five-bit range.

So the adder never loses anything: its output width is sufficient for every input it can be given. Results are lost only when a designer wires four of the five pins onward and leaves the carry out unconnected, which is a decision made outside the adder.

sections.title: Subtraction without a subtractor
sections.body:
In two's complement, negating a number means inverting every bit and adding one. So A − B is A + (NOT B) + 1 — and an adder can do all of it, provided something can invert B on demand and something can supply the +1.

Both jobs are already available. An XOR gate with one input tied to a control line is a controlled inverter: with the control at 0 it passes its data input through unchanged, with the control at 1 it inverts it. And the +1 goes into the carry in of stage 0, the pin that was tied to 0 for plain addition.

One control line, called SUB, therefore turns a four-bit adder into a four-bit adder-subtractor: it feeds all four XOR gates and the carry in at once.

questions.prompt: With the SUB line at 0, what does the XOR gate in each B path do?

choices.text: Passes B through unchanged — B ⊕ 0 = B.
Forces its output to 0, disconnecting B from the adder.
Inverts B, which is why SUB must be 1 for ordinary addition.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: XOR with 0 is the identity, and XOR with 1 is inversion. That single property is the whole trick: one gate per bit converts the adder between its two modes with no multiplexer and no second datapath.

responses.title: That would be an AND gate.
responses.body: AND with 0 does force the output to 0 — and an adder fed all-zero B would just return A, which is a useful circuit but not this one. XOR leaves its data input alone when the control is 0.

responses.title: It is the other way round.
responses.body: SUB = 0 is addition and SUB = 1 is subtraction, which is also why SUB can drive the carry in directly: the same 1 that inverts B supplies the +1 that two's complement needs.

verify.caption: Verify — the controlled inverter at rest
verify.note: B = 1 with SUB = 0: the output reads 1, unchanged. Set the SUB slider to 1 in Figure 11.1 and the same input reads 0.

questions.prompt: Why does the SUB line also drive the carry input of stage 0?

choices.text: It supplies the +1 that two's complement negation needs after inverting B.
To signal to the adder that it is in subtract mode, so the stages reverse their arithmetic.
To make the borrow propagate leftward instead of the carry.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Inverting B gives the one's complement; two's complement is that plus one, and the carry in of the least significant stage is a free +1 that costs no extra hardware. Both halves of the negation are done by wires that already existed.

responses.title: The full adders have no modes.
responses.body: Every stage does exactly the same thing it always did: add three bits. The entire difference between adding and subtracting lives outside them, in four XOR gates and the carry-in wire.

responses.title: There is no separate borrow path.
responses.body: That is the elegance of the method: the subtractor has no borrow logic at all, because a borrow in two's complement IS the absence of a carry. The carry out of the top stage reads 1 when A ≥ B and 0 when a borrow would have been needed.

worked.why: Write down what subtraction becomes. Two’s complement turns A − B into an addition, so nothing new has to be computed: invert every bit of B, then add one. The circuit does the inversion with four XOR gates and the +1 with the carry in.
Invert B. B = 0110, so each bit flips. This intermediate value is the one’s complement, and on its own it is not −6 — it is one short, which is what the next step supplies.

Add, with the carry in at 1. Column 0: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, so S0 = 1 and a carry goes up. Column 1: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2, so S1 = 0, carry up. Column 2: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, so S2 = 1, no carry. Column 3: 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, so S3 = 0 and the carry leaves the adder.
Read the four sum bits. The fifth bit is the carry out and is not part of the numeric result — in subtract mode it is the borrow flag, and a 1 means no borrow was needed.

Check both halves. 11 − 6 = 5, and the carry out of 1 confirms A ≥ B, so 0101 is a plain positive five rather than a two’s-complement pattern. Figure 11.2 reads exactly these five pins — 0101 with the carry out at 1. Drag its SUB slider to 0 and the same circuit returns 0001 with a carry out of 1, which is 11 + 6 = 17.

figures.caption: Figure 11.1 — an XOR gate as a controlled inverter
figures.note: Press Simulate, then drag SUB. With SUB at 0 the output follows B; with SUB at 1 it is the opposite of B. The table below confirms both columns by simulation.

figures.caption: Figure 11.2 — a four-bit adder-subtractor computing 1011 − 0110
figures.note: Press Simulate. The sum outputs read 0101 — five, which is 11 − 6 — and the carry out reads 1, meaning no borrow was needed. Drag SUB to 0 and the same circuit computes 11 + 6 = 17 instead: 0001 with the carry out still at 1.

sections.after: Reading the carry out in subtract mode. It inverts its usual meaning: 1 means A ≥ B and the result is a plain positive number, while 0 means a borrow — the true answer is negative and the pins hold its two's-complement form. This is why processors distinguish 'carry' from 'borrow' in their documentation while using one physical flag for both.

problems.prompt: Set the adder-subtractor to compute 0110 − 1011 (six minus eleven). What do the pins read, and how should the result be interpreted?
problems.answer:
Invert 1011 to get 0100, then add: 0110 + 0100 + 1 = 1011, with a carry out of 0.

The zero carry out is the borrow: the true answer is negative. Reading 1011 as two's complement gives −5, which is correct, since 6 − 11 = −5. Nothing has failed — the circuit has produced a signed result and told you, on the carry pin, that you should read it as one.

verify.caption: Verify — 0110 − 1011
verify.note: The sum outputs read 1011 and the carry out reads 0. As an unsigned pattern that is eleven; as two's complement it is −5, which is the answer.

problems.prompt: Compute 1001 − 1100 (nine minus twelve) on the same circuit, by hand first.
problems.answer:
Invert 1100 to get 0011, then add with the extra 1: 1001 + 0011 + 1 = 1101, carry out 0.

Borrow again, so read 1101 as signed: −3. And 9 − 12 = −3. Note how little the circuit cares about the sizes involved — it performs the same four-column addition either way, and the carry out is the only thing that changes meaning.

verify.caption: Verify — 1001 − 1100
verify.note: 1101 on the sum pins, carry out 0 — a borrow, and a signed answer of −3.

sections.title: Putting the answer on a display
sections.body:
Four sum bits are an answer only to someone who reads binary. A BCD-to-seven-segment driver turns a four-bit value into the seven segment signals that spell that digit, and a seven-segment display lights them.

The circuit below is the adder of §7 with its sum bits taken to a driver instead of stopping at the output pins: three plus four, and the display shows a 7. Nothing about the adder changed — the bits it produced were always a number; this is just the first figure that says so in a font.

Only one digit. A single display shows 0 to 9, and a four-bit adder can reach 15. Feed it 1010 or above and the driver has no digit to show — real designs convert the binary result to BCD first, with a converter that is itself built from adders.

figures.caption: Figure 12.1 — three plus four, shown as a digit
figures.note: Press Simulate: the sum outputs read 0111 and the display lights the segments for 7. Drag the sliders to change either number — but keep the total below 10, or the driver has nothing to show.

problems.prompt: The A inputs are changed to 0001 while B stays at 0100. What do the sum pins read, and what appears on the display?
problems.answer:
1 + 4 = 5, so the sum pins read 0101 and the display shows a 5. The driver lights segments a, c, d, f and g to draw it — the same five segments a calculator uses, chosen by a small block of combinational logic no more mysterious than the adder feeding it.

Everything in this lesson is now in one chain: gates make a half adder, half adders make a full adder, full adders chain into a four-bit adder, and a decoder turns the result into something a person can read.

verify.caption: Verify — one plus four
verify.note: The sum pins read 0101 and the display draws a 5.

sections.title: Problem set
sections.body: Six problems over the whole lesson. Work each on paper before opening its answer; where the answer can be settled by a circuit, it carries one you can run.

figures.caption: Figure 13.1 — which adder a column of bits needs
figures.script:
diagram("direction: down
(How many bits, and is speed critical?) as start
<Just one column, with nothing carried in?> as one
[Half adder: XOR and AND] as ha #mint
<Does a carry arrive from the right?> as chain
[Full adder: the general column] as fa #blue
<Is the width small, or the clock slow?> as wide
[Ripple-carry: n full adders, delay 2n+1 gates] as ripple #blue
[Carry-lookahead: carries computed from the inputs, more gates, near-constant delay] as cla #amber
start -> one
one -> ha : yes
one -> chain : no
chain -> fa : yes
fa -> wide
wide -> ripple : yes
wide -> cla : no");
figures.note: Carry-lookahead is named here for completeness and is not built in these notes — it is the standard answer to §9's delay problem, and the next lesson's subject.

problems.prompt: 1. How many full adders does a 16-bit adder need, and how many gates is that if each full adder is built from two half adders and an OR?
problems.answer:
Sixteen full adders, one per bit column. Each is two half adders (two XOR gates and two AND gates) plus one OR: five gates each, so 80 gates in total.

Worth comparing against the delay: 80 gates buys a circuit that takes (2 × 16 + 1) = 33 gate delays to settle. A carry-lookahead version of the same width costs several times the gates and settles in a small constant number of delays — the usual trade of area for time, made explicit.

problems.prompt: 2. A four-bit adder is given A = 1100, B = 1010, carry in 0. Give the sum bits and carry out, and check the result in decimal both as unsigned and as signed values.
problems.answer:
Column 0: 0 + 0 = 0. Column 1: 0 + 1 = 1. Column 2: 1 + 0 = 1. Column 3: 1 + 1 = 2, so S3 = 0 and the carry leaves. The pins read 0110 with a carry out of 1.

Unsigned: 12 + 10 = 22, and 10110 is 22 — correct across five bits. Signed: 1100 is −4 and 1010 is −6, so the answer should be −10; the pins read 0110, which is +6, and V = C4 ⊕ C3 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. Two negatives gave a positive, so the signed result has overflowed while the unsigned one is fine.

problems.prompt: 3. Why can a half adder not be used for the most significant column of a multi-bit adder, even though there is no carry to produce beyond it?
problems.answer:
Because of the carry coming IN, not the carry going out. The top column still receives a carry from the column below it, and a half adder has no input for it — the bit would simply be dropped and every result that carried into the top column would be wrong by eight (in a four-bit adder).

The column that genuinely can use a half adder is the LEAST significant one, whose carry in is tied to 0 — and many textbook diagrams do exactly that, saving one OR gate and one XOR gate at the bottom of the chain. This lesson's figures use a full adder everywhere so the stages are identical, which matters more in silicon than two gates do.

problems.prompt: 4. An adder-subtractor computes A − B and its carry out reads 1. What does that tell you about A and B, and what would a carry out of 0 have meant?
problems.answer:
A carry out of 1 means A ≥ B: no borrow was needed and the sum pins hold the plain positive difference. A carry out of 0 means a borrow — A < B, and the pins hold the two's-complement form of a negative answer.

This is also a comparator for free. Feed A and B into an adder-subtractor, ignore the sum bits entirely, and the carry out alone answers "is A at least B?" in the time it takes a carry to ripple.

problems.prompt: 5. Each gate switches in 1.5 ns. A designer replaces a four-bit ripple-carry adder with two four-bit adders in parallel, one assuming a carry in of 0 and one assuming 1, and selects between their results with a multiplexer once the real carry arrives. Why does that help at all — and what has it cost?
problems.answer:
Both halves start computing immediately, so the wait for the real carry is spent doing useful work instead of idling. The result is ready one multiplexer delay after the carry arrives — roughly 9Δ + 1Δ rather than the 9Δ + 9Δ of two chained four-bit adders — so an eight-bit sum takes about 15 ns instead of 25.5 ns.

The cost is silicon: two adders and a multiplexer per block instead of one adder. This structure is called carry-select, and it is the same bargain as carry-lookahead written a different way — spend area to stop waiting.

problems.prompt: 6. Show that a full adder can be used as a three-input "count the ones" circuit, and say what its two outputs mean when read that way.
problems.answer:
The full adder's outputs are the two-bit binary count of how many of its three inputs are 1: carry out is the twos place and sum is the ones place. 000 → 00, one input high → 01, two high → 10, three high → 11.

Used this way it is called a 3:2 compressor, and it is the heart of fast multipliers: a tree of them reduces many partial products to two numbers in a few gate delays, and only the final pair needs a real carry-propagating adder. The same five gates, asked a different question.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Every circuit in this lesson was simulated, not asserted: the truth tables were generated by running the gates, and every figure's outputs were read off the solver. Six statements carry the rest.

  1. 1 + 1 = 10. A one-bit addition needs two outputs, a sum and a carry, and that is why adders exist at all.
  2. The half adder is S = A ⊕ B, C = A · B — complete for the least significant column, useless for any other, because it has no carry input.
  3. The full adder is S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), and it is exactly two half adders with their carries ORed.
  4. Ripple-carry chains them, one per bit, and costs (2n + 1) gate delays — linear in the width, which is why wide fast adders are built differently.
  5. The carry out answers the unsigned question only. Signed overflow is V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1: same-signed operands producing the opposite sign.
  6. Subtraction is free. Four XOR gates and the carry in turn the adder into an adder-subtractor, because A − B is A + NOT B + 1.
Next in this courseCarry-lookahead and fast adders: computing every carry directly from the inputs with generate and propagate terms, so the delay stops growing with the width — the answer to §9's 97.5 ns.
